articles.title: Find the Zigbee devices that need attention
articles.dek: A single overview separates offline devices and unfinished setup from weak signals, low batteries and pending updates.
body: A sensor that only works some of the time should not require opening every device page to find the weak link. Home Assistant adds a Network health page to its ZHA Zigbee panel, showing the spread of strong, fair, weak and offline connections across the home.

Devices that are offline or never finished setup appear with their area, power source and last contact. Separate lists flag weak connections, low batteries and available firmware updates, grouped by room with the worst readings first. Disabled devices stay out of the attention count.

Robert makes his first contribution to the frontend with the page, following Matthias de Baat’s design direction. Signal strength uses neighbouring devices’ reports where possible, falling back to the last received packet when those reports are unavailable. The overview exposes existing measurements; it does not repair the network automatically.

pullRequests.title: Add network health page to ZHA panel

media.alt: The ZHA Network health page with network quality and devices needing attention.

articles.title: A household assistant would stay off until you choose it
articles.dek: Revised plans separate AI from Voice, with saved chats and a significant change to typed home control.
body: People who do not want AI should be able to leave it off without removing individual integrations. Home Assistant is shaping a separate household assistant and settings area: choosing a provider would not automatically enable suggestions, and the interface would not keep prompting people to turn them on.

Niels argued for hiding AI features until a provider is configured. The revised proposals would identify local and cloud providers, ask for a provider and model, and supply the other model settings. Existing AI Task configurations would retain their enabled state; the new household assistant would have its own off-by-default switch, separate from Assist and its voice settings.

A proposed panel would stay beside the current page on desktop and use a bottom sheet on mobile. The page address would help it understand questions about “this automation”; conversations would be saved per person across devices, with controls to reopen or delete them. Marcin Bauer argued for being able to retrieve a chat after closing its dialog. Reading the current configuration is in scope; editing it is not.

The planned split would remove text input from the Assist dialog, leaving households without an AI provider unable to use that route for typed home control. These proposals remain in Shaping. Conversation retention, administrators’ access to other people’s history and whether the fixed model settings work well locally remain open design questions.

articles.title: An assistant can inspect failures and work through repairs
articles.dek: Administrators gain access to saved automation runs and supported fix forms; permission to change settings remains separate from diagnosis.
body: A light that did not turn on can leave a trail showing which condition or action stopped the routine. Home Assistant gives connected AI assistants the saved runs of automations and scripts, including the steps of a chosen run, alongside their configuration and the shared templates they use.

Niels opened a related proposal for administrator-only diagnostic access. Markus Tuominen mapped the existing tools and gaps; Niels credited Paulus Schoutsen and Allen Porter with building the foundation. The new trace tools address one of those gaps, without changing the trace viewer or guaranteeing that a model will identify every fault.

Where an assistant has permission to make changes, Allen Porter also adds tools to work through supported repair forms and menus. Only active, visible notices marked as fixable qualify. Repairs can remove configuration or restart equipment, and an external sign-in step sends the person back to the Repairs page.

The diagnostic proposal remains in Shaping and calls for read-only access. The broader management connection also contains tools that make changes; an external assistant connection needs its read-only option enabled to exclude those tools.

articles.title: A damaged web update no longer leaves a board unable to start
articles.dek: ESP8266 protection covers ordinary firmware files; compressed uploads still lack the same check.
body: An update that loses bytes on the way to a device can look successful while leaving it unable to boot. ESPHome checks the completed firmware image before installing it through an ESP8266 web server or captive portal, rejecting a damaged file instead of replacing the working software.

The failure was reproduced on a D1 mini by removing about seven kilobytes from an upload. Recovery required a cable and a fresh installation. Native updates and updates fetched by the device already include a separate integrity check; ESP32 has its own validation.
The new check applies to uncompressed files. A compressed .bin.gz web upload remains outside it.

pullRequests.title: [ota] Reject an ESP8266 web upload that lost bytes instead of flashing it

articles.title: The first boot skips a second software download
articles.dek: The installer puts Core and plugins into the system image, increasing the initial download and USB requirements.
body: A freshly installed device can start Home Assistant without first downloading Core. The installer switches its ordinary installation flows to full operating-system images that already contain Core and its plugins, moving that download into the initial installation.

Robert Resch verifies the signed image list against the expected operating-system version before installation. A board whose matching image is not ready receives a retryable error. Core inside the image can be older than the latest version, which Supervisor then offers as an update.
The full images are about three times the download size, and the live USB stick needs 4 GB. Resetting a Green or a Yellow with a CM4 remains on the separate pinned installer path.

pullRequests.title: Install HAOS with Home Assistant preloaded alias full images

articles.title: Long Apple Music tracks start without the long wait
articles.dek: A measured 13-minute recording begins in about a second through Sendspin.
body: Choosing a long recording could mean waiting seven or eight seconds before hearing it. Music Assistant skips an unnecessary scan of Apple Music’s audio stream, so a longer track no longer creates a proportionally longer silence at the start.

In Marvin Schenkel’s lab, an 814-second track reached a Sendspin player in 0.7–1.1 seconds, down from 7.1–8.4 seconds from a stopped queue. The audio matched the previous output exactly. Those figures describe that stream and test setup; they are not a timing guarantee for every connection.

pullRequests.title: Fix Apple Music start delay that grows with track length

articles.title: Your uploaded songs join the music library
articles.dek: Personal albums and artists no longer need a playlist detour to appear.
body: A recording uploaded to YouTube Music lives outside that service’s regular library. Music Assistant’s sync now reads that separate collection too, importing its songs, albums and artists instead of finding them only when someone opens a playlist.
The upload remains tied to the account that supplied it. Artist entries resolve through the uploaded collection, while untagged recordings retain the existing Music Library Uploads fallback.

pullRequests.title: Sync uploaded YouTube Music music into the library

articles.title: Ignore Zigbee devices you cannot reset
articles.dek: A new blocklist suppresses rediscovery, but cannot prevent every kind of radio traffic.
body: A removed device that cannot be reset—such as a neighbour’s device—can keep reappearing on a Zigbee network. Zigpy adds a list of device addresses to ignore, asking each blocked device to leave when it turns up again.

The setting can pass through ZHA’s existing Zigpy configuration once the updated library is included. A device already listed still needs to be removed normally; blocking it does not delete the existing entry.

This is not a security boundary. A device that ignores the request still has the network key and can communicate directly with other devices. Green Power devices, which follow a different joining process, are not covered.

pullRequests.title: Add a `blocked_devices` option to ignore devices and ask them to leave

articles.title: Require a trusted device certificate for remote access
articles.dek: The extra Link check is optional and uses the certificates already configured in network settings.
body: A remote connection can be refused before it opens unless the connecting client presents an accepted certificate. Home Assistant adds this option to Link remote access, using the client-certificate configuration from the network settings.

Javier Torres keeps the requirement off by default, preserving existing connections unless the owner enables it. This adds a certificate requirement to that remote route; it does not configure certificates for the owner’s devices.

pullRequests.title: Allow requiring client certificates in Link remote connection
Document 'Require client certificates for remote access' option

articles.title: Small displays regain their missing text and pictures
articles.dek: Related corrections cover blank grayscale interfaces and images that became solid blocks.
body: A custom control panel could show a black screen even though its interface was being drawn. ESPHome corrects how four grayscale display drivers interpret brightness, restoring visible text and controls from LVGL, the library used to build those interfaces.

A companion correction separates picture transparency from colour, preventing black pixels lighting up on monochrome screens and grayscale images becoming solid white. Clyde Stubbs checked the image correction on an SSD1306 display. The grayscale-driver change has automated coverage but no grayscale-panel hardware test; the older Waveshare e-paper component can display the corrected images as negatives.

articles.title: Interrupt a waiting reply and ask again
articles.dek: Voice Preview Edition can leave its answering animation promptly when playback has not started.
body: Pressing stop while an answer was still being prepared could leave a voice satellite busy for up to fifteen seconds. ESPHome finishes that cancelled response immediately, allowing the wake word to begin another conversation instead of waiting for a playback timeout.

In Maxi1134’s Voice Preview Edition test, stopping before audio began returned the device to idle in 29 milliseconds, compared with 12.1 seconds in the earlier comparison. The spoken-stop test used additional voice firmware; the centre button already exercises the affected path. This is Maxi1134’s first contribution to ESPHome.

pullRequests.title: [voice_assistant] Finish a response stopped before playback starts

articles.title: Large dashboard cards arrive as one download
articles.dek: Marketplace preserves supporting folders and checks the complete package before installing it.
body: A complex community card can include dozens of scripts, translations and images. Home Assistant’s Marketplace can install these together from a matching ZIP release asset, keeping the folder structure instead of downloading each file separately.

Wendelin validates file paths, sizes and contents before writing the package. An unusable ZIP falls back to a working JavaScript release asset when available; if there is no fallback, installation fails and restores the previous version. A catalog entry with only a ZIP also avoids the GitHub API request used to list separate release assets.
Card authors must name the ZIP after their dashboard resource. Installing directly from a repository branch or commit keeps the existing single-file route.

pullRequests.title: Install Marketplace dashboard cards shipped as a ZIP release
Document ZIP releases for Marketplace dashboard cards

articles.title: Custom wake words need a new home
articles.dek: Linux satellites separate bundled, downloaded and personal models; old paths are ignored.
body: People who supply their own wake-word models need to move them into Linux Voice Assistant’s new directory layout. Custom models belong under custom/microwakeword or custom/openwakeword beneath the wake-word root; the supplied container setup provides a separate custom-model volume.

The root is configured with --wake-word-root-dir or WAKE_WORD_ROOT_DIR. Old location options are accepted only with a warning and ignored, so the satellite still starts but its personal wake words can go missing until the setup is changed.

Models from different sources and recognition engines also become separate entries instead of silently replacing one another. The Voice Support app does not yet recognize the expanded names for its extra wake-word verification; requests continue without that check.

pullRequests.title: Wake word directory layout with internal, downloaded and custom

articles.title: Alarm automations need the new UniFi arm profiles
articles.dek: Protect 7.4’s global alarm manager replaces the old NVR panel on affected consoles.
body: An automation targeting the old Alarm Manager panel needs to select its replacement after a console moves to UniFi’s global alarm manager. Home Assistant creates an alarm control panel for each arm profile and removes the old NVR panel only on those consoles.
Profiles added or removed on the console appear without a manual reload. Entry delay appears as pending and a breach as triggered; other consoles retain their existing NVR panel.

pullRequests.title: Add alarm control panels for UniFi Protect external arm profiles

articles.title: A broken music provider can still offer its repair
articles.dek: Marketplace shows updates even when an installed extension cannot start.
body: A community provider that stops loading after a Music Assistant upgrade could hide the very update that fixes it. The Marketplace now shows the newer version and an Update button even while the provider is not running.
Those updates also appear in Check for changes and Update all. This restores the normal update route; it does not promise that every available version will solve the underlying incompatibility.

articles.title: More sensor data fits into a short radio message
articles.dek: Matching dictionaries shrink text before transmission; both devices need the same configuration.
body: A long list of readings can exceed a radio’s packet limit even when it contains mostly familiar field names. ESPHome adds optional compression to its device-to-device packet links, using a shared dictionary to shorten that repeated text.

In Clyde Stubbs’s four-minute LoRa test, a device list of 402–405 bytes became 81–104 bytes. All 123 messages accepted for transmission arrived intact in both directions. Those results used a dictionary made from a typical message; they are not a general compression guarantee.
Messages that do not shrink are sent without compression. A mismatched dictionary causes a packet to be rejected rather than delivered as incorrect data.

articles.title: Pause the music while your assistant speaks
articles.dek: Linux satellites can resume only after overlapping conversations and timers finish.
body: A voice reply does not have to compete with music playing quietly underneath it. Linux Voice Assistant adds an optional pause mode for its music player during replies, announcements and ringing timers; lowering the volume remains the default.

Each reason for quieting the music is tracked separately, so stopping a timer does not restore the volume in the middle of a conversation. Already-paused music stays paused, and a person’s playback command takes precedence over automatic resuming.

Set --mpv-player-duck-mode pause, or MPV_PLAYER_DUCK_MODE=pause, to use it. Music started while the assistant is already interrupting it still plays at full volume, a documented limitation. The source reports unit tests rather than a microphone-and-speaker trial.

pullRequests.title: Keep the music ducked until every reason for ducking is over
Add option to pause the music instead of lowering it while ducking

articles.title: Short announcements reach sleeping Cast players
articles.dek: Preparing every speaker first adds a brief wait when a group starts from idle.
body: A Nest Hub joining a Sendspin group could miss an entire spoken announcement while its playback app started. Music Assistant launches the app on every Cast speaker in the group together and waits for their clocks to be ready before sending the sound.

The wait is capped at ten seconds; a failed or slow speaker does not hold the others indefinitely. In the reported Nest Hub checks, a previously silent ten-second group clip and a 1.5-second solo clip both played. A cold start takes about one extra second for a single speaker or three seconds for the tested group.

pullRequests.title: Let Cast speakers in a Sendspin group play short sounds from the start

articles.title: Local apps survive backup encryption and decryption
articles.dek: Archive names now match the folders used by locally installed apps.
body: A locally installed app’s archive could be missed when Home Assistant encrypted or decrypted a backup because its folder and archive used different separators in the name. The backup code matches those names correctly.

@sannapaulsson makes a first contribution to Core with the correction and verified that both archives restored with their original contents. The change concerns local app archives rather than changing the backup’s encryption settings.

pullRequests.title: Fix local add-on handling in backup encryption and decryption
